item.title: The Giant Measurement at the End of Time
item.description:
2.5.6.0.1 Kent and Bousso&Susskind have proposed approaches to defining quantum wavefunction branches based on late-time information. The basic idea is to exploit the way that quantum information propagates in our universe in particular: (a) photons(and gravitons) carry away information at the speed of light, (b) the universe is expanding and cooling, meaning that these photons(in some cosmological environments) may propagate uninterruptedly forever.

2.5.6.0.2 What this means is that photons very late in time are a privileged set of degrees of freedom: they plausibly carry information about everything that has classically "happened" previously. This suggests a way of defining the set of branches: just "measure"(apply a fictitious measurement operator, that is) the photon degrees of freedom very late in time!

2.5.6.0.3 That's the basic idea. There are many subtleties of course, and Kent and Bousso/Susskind have different proposals. I'll review each in turn and then talk about the philosophical merit of these approaches in general.

  • 2.5.6.0.3.1 The following discussion uses some elementary definitions of objects from general relativity. If you know what a spacelike surface and lightcone are, that should be enough.
  • 2.5.6.0.3.2* Note that as of the time of writing, QFTs in arbitrary space-times are not totally mathematically well-defined objects -- and what's more, the fully correct theory of the objects we are discussing should be quantum gravitational, where we don't even know what the exact form of the theory should look like. Thus these constructions are a bit sketchily defined, even compared to QFTs which are already mathematically sketchy.

2.5.6.1 Quantum Reality via Late-Time Photodetection

2.5.6.1.1 Kent has proposed a few variants of this idea. I'll review the version in his paper Quantum Reality via Late-Time Photodetection.

2.5.6.1.2 Kent is interested in defining a set of possible histories of what he calls "beables", which are essentially the classical-like variables which we think of as defining a possible world, e.g. the positions of objects.

2.5.6.1.3 For his set of beables Kent considers the expected values of quantum observables at a given time, conditioned on some particular late-time outcome of photodetection measurements across all of space(with an additional subtlety I'll get to momentarily).

2.5.6.1.4 Why does this make sense? The idea is that the late-time photons should contain all the information about possible classical experiments, pinning down a possible quantum state associated with a set of measurement outcomes. The expected values then give us the classical-like variables associated with this set. Taking the expected value is necessary because even in a classical-like world all degrees of freedom will still be "spread out" in a quantum manner to some degree.

  • 2.5.6.1.4.1 For example, if we consider a covalently-bonded molecule, its position might be decohered by a measurement and thus ultimately correlated with late-time photons. However, the internal state of the electrons in the covalent bond may not be. So if we condition on late time photons, the position of the molecule will be approximately fixed, but the positions of the electrons will not. Taking the expected value of the probability of detecting an electron in a given place will give a spread out "blob" around the covalent bond. This gives the quasi-classical state we are looking for.

2.5.6.1.5 Now, however, a problem arises. If we project onto an entire late-time space-like surface, this is correlated with the results of all past experiments. This means that the beables at a given point in time will be conditioned on the results of experiments in that point's future, which may give strange results.

  • 2.5.6.1.5.1 For example, say that some time later we take our molecule from the previous experiment and measure the position of the electrons in the covalent bond. The results of this experiment will be recorded in some late-time photons. So if we condition on all these photons, the electrons' positions will be decohered at earlier points as well! In other words, when we consider the expected value of the electrons' position earlier, we will no longer find them in a "blob" corresponding to a normal covalent bond, but rather a state which will evolve to whatever position measurement we end up sampling.

2.5.6.1.6 Clearly, this is undesirable. Kent's solution is to restrict the set of photodetection results we condition on in the future space-like surface. For a given point in spacetime p, we only condition on points on this surface outside the forward light cone of p.

  • 2.5.6.1.6.1 In the molecule example, if we consider a point before we measure the electrons' position, the future experiment, and hence all photons downstream of it, are in the forward light-cone. So these experimental results would not be conditioned on, restoring the normal covalent bond.
  • 2.5.6.1.6.2 This means that measured systems will "collapse" to a given value slightly after they have been measured. In particular, this will occur once there are outgoing photons spacelike separated from the system.
  • 2.5.6.1.6.3 Note however, that we still sample a single shared set of measurement outcomes for all points in spacetime; it's just that when defining the beables at a particular point, we only condition on the outcomes outside of the forward light cone. This ensures we define a consistent shared reality.

2.5.6.1.7 So in summary, Kent's prescription for defining a set of quasiclassical worlds and their probabilities is as follows: given some initial quantum state on a spacelike surface, we evolve it forward until some late-time spacelike surface. We then measure the state of photons on this surface, obtaining a particular set of measurement values defining a quasiclassical world. The quasiclassical "beables" at a given point p in spacetime between these two surfaces are defined to be the expected values of quantum observables(Kent uses the values of the stress-energy tensor) conditioned on the portion of these measurements outside the forward-light cone of p.

  • 2.5.6.1.7.1 To define such a history for the entire universe, and remove the dependence on choice of surface, Kent takes the limit as the spacelike surface is evolved to future infinity. Given our cosmology(an increasingly empty and sparse universe) it seems plausible that this gives rise to a well-defined limit. There are also various other technicalities I won't get into here.

2.5.6.2 The Multiverse Interpretation of Quantum Mechanics

2.5.6.2.1 Bousso and Susskind defined a related construction in their paper The Multiverse Interpretation of Quantum Mechanics, initially motivated by the problem of defining measurement outcomes in an inflationary multiverse.

2.5.6.2.2 They consider both a local and global construction; the global construction is a limit of local constructions so let's talk about the local construction first. The idea is to consider the possible experiments that can be conducted by a local observer, using what's called a causal diamond.

2.5.6.2.3 What's a causal diamond? It's essentially defined by gluing together a forward and backwards lightcone. In more detail, if we have a point p in spacetime and a point q in its future, we consider the future lightcone of p and the backwards lightcone of q. These meet at a spacelike surface S; the causal diamond is the union of the interiors of the forward and backwards lightcone up until S.

2.5.6.2.4 Any finite experiment carried out by an observer lives in some causal diamond. Why is this? If we consider an observer who evolves from a point p in spacetime to a later point q, any effect the observer can have, for instance setting up a measurement device, lies in the future lightcone of p. And any information that they can observe lies in the past lightcone of q. Thus the effects they can observe from a given experiment are determined by the sequence of quantum states inside the diamond.

2.5.6.2.5 This means that the future boundary of the causal diamond(i.e. the part consisting of the backwards lightcone) provides an objective choice of "environment" to condition on when considering the results of experiments performed in the diamond.

  • 2.5.6.2.5.1 Note that conditioning on photon states on the boundary may also decohere events outside of the diamond in its causal past. For example, we can run an experiment on Earth measuring the cosmic microwave background. This is correlated with quantum events in the distant past, but photons leaving our local causal diamond contain enough information to decohere them(due to correlations of our measuring apparatus, brains etc. with the events). A finite diamond will generally not have enough information on its future boundary to decohere all classical-like events in its past, however.

2.5.6.2.6 So this gives us a local objective notion of decoherence. The causal diamond also has the nice feature that it defines a branch-like structure on the set of possible measurement results. We can consider information that has left the future boundary up until a given point. For instance, say we measure a system, wait a bit, then perform further measurements on the same system. The photons associated with the first measurement will leave the causal diamond's future boundary before the photons associated with the second.


2.5.6.2.7 How do we extend this to a global picture? The idea is to consider an indefinitely long-lived observer, and take the limit of diamonds defined by a sequence of points on their future trajectory. This will produce a sequence of diamonds of unbounded area(in asymptotically flat universes). Some photons will escape the sequence of diamonds -- aka, for any diamond, some time evolution of the photon's state will be on the boundary. We may equivalently say that these photons escape to null infinity(which is simply the space of possible unbounded photon trajectories). Conditioning on these photon states provides a limiting notion of decoherence and branching for the past of the limiting causal diamond.

  • 2.5.6.2.7.1 In what sense is this a global picture? For an indefinitely long-lived observer in an asymptotically flat universe, their past light cone eventually includes every location in their universe[1]. So every location in spacetime is eventually included in the volume that can potentially be decohered by the limiting photons.
  • 2.5.6.2.7.2 This construction doesn't apply to non-asymptotically flat spacetimes. In universes with a positive cosmological constant, observers' past lightcones don't eventually include everything, as accelerating expansion means an increasing volume of spacetime is forever out of their reach. In this case the future boundary of the diamond approaches a cosmic horizon with finite entropy.
  • 2.5.6.2.7.3 Our universe appears to be of this type, with a (very tiny) positive cosmological constant. That said, it's not out of the question that the apparent c.c. is actually time-dependent(due to quintessence say) and decaying to zero. And there are ways to try adapting the construction to non-asymptotically-flat universes.

2.5.6.2.8 The use of the order in which photons escape to define a branching order bears some resemblance to Kent's proposal to define beables via conditioning only on future events outside a point's future lightcone. If we consider an observer evolving forward in time through a Kentian multiverse, they condition on an increasingly large portion of the future surface. This defines a tree-like structure on the set of possible worlds, which seems plausibly equivalent to that defined by Bousso & Susskind's construction in the limit of the future surface approaching infinity.

2.5.6.3 General Discussion

2.5.6.3.1 So that's my preferred family of definitions of wavefunction branches. Why do I like them?

2.5.6.3.2 First of all, they are plausibly correct. That is, it's plausible that, given a quantum state corresponding to our early universe, if you applied the time evolution operator followed by a late-time photon measurement operator, you would in fact get the set of states and probabilities corresponding to what we intuitively think of as quasiclassical worlds. I know of no other proposed definition that seems as likely to me to meet this bar.

2.5.6.3.3 Secondly, they are elegant. The set of worlds is defined by a single measurement, using the standard quantum definition of measurement. The branching structure is determined by a sequence of measurements, themselves determined by geometrically natural constructs from relativity. There are no arbitrary constants.

2.5.6.3.4 "Isn't the retroactive nature of the construct kinda wacky?" Any definition of wavefunction branching will have at least a bit of a retroactive character, because isolated systems can only be said to have decohered/branched some time after their initial interaction with the environment has sufficiently propagated records/increased the complexity.

2.5.6.3.5 Here's a general argument against any definition of wavefunction branching that doesn't rely on some sort of asymptotic late-time measurement. Say we have a definition based on (e.g.) number of copies of records, or circuit complexity. Then it would be possible for a sufficiently technologically advanced civilization to "spoof" the definition by conducting an experiment in which they evolve an isolated quantum system to meet the definition, then reverse the evolution. According to the definition, branches would form and then re-merge! A set of branches in a sensible definition should never do this.

2.5.6.3.6 This concludes my account of the problem of defining wavefunction branches/the measurement problem. Now what does this have to do with our original goal of explaining the relation between the laws of physics and the existence of life/sentience?

  • 2.5.6.3.6.1 The full answer is complicated and will occupy much of the rest of the blog. But basically, the idea is that quantum mechanics combines two features: observations are defined by information copying, or Darwinism, or propagation of influence. And yet at the same time, the state of the system being measured/copied is to some degree sensitive to the context/basis in which it is measured. The measurements are chained together to form an irreversible history. I think these features recur in many other contexts in our world.
  • 2.5.6.3.6.2 But first I'll briefly go over some more aspects of physics that strike me as potentially relevant re: life and sentience.
  1. ^

    Although, as Bousso & Susskind discuss in their paper, if the asymptotically flat universe is merely a bubble in an inflationary multiverse, the past light cone will not eventually include everything in this wider universe. It will include everything in the bubble's past lightcone. They discuss a proposal to define observables in the rest of the multiverse via "hat complementarity", in analogy with black hole complementarity.

item.title: Could Insurance Companies Help with AI Safety?
item.description:
Epistemic Status: Rough Fermi model, numbers could be off by an order of magnitude, probably not multiple orders of magnitude. Definitely interested in feedback on assumptions you'd change.

Long-time lurker here. I think I last posted in about 2010. I've been reading various pieces (here, for example) on whether insurance companies can help solve a conflict of interest problem in AI Safety, and I thought I'd play around with building a simplified insurance pricing model to see if it helped put any numbers on the plausibility of the plan.

TL;DR I think this could be a good idea, but:

  1. Premiums will be trivial vs lab revenue, so this will probably only work with state compulsion - it won't fly as a "pure" private sector solution to conflicts of interest in AI safety monitoring.
  2. Even if insurers are directly writing policies for frontier firms, and imposing safety policies on them, the numbers suggest insurers are going to be more focussed on more "mundane" risks than the ones that face society as a whole.
  3. Insurers profit from cutting liability, which isn't always the same as harm.

I'd be interested to get feedback on the analysis below (it's cross-posted from Substack). The words in this essay are my own, but the words on my accompanying model explainer website are mostly Claude's.


Anthropic’s Form S-1 filing mentions the difficulty of getting insurance coverage for the type of risks they face.

From page 50:

Our insurance policies also may not provide sufficient coverage to adequately mitigate the potential liabilities we face, especially where any one incident, or a group of incidents, causes disproportionate harm. In addition, with the scale of harm that could result from a catastrophic AI-related incident, no single insurer, and potentially the insurance industry in the aggregate, may have sufficient capacity or expertise to underwrite insurance commensurate with such exposure.

This sounds very plausible, these are expensive events for insurance firms to cover. The risks could range from AI enhanced cyber attacks, through to AI engineered biological weapons and full loss-of-control scenarios resulting in mass loss-of-life. Nonetheless, I thought it would be interesting to try to put some numbers to try to distinguish perils that feasibly could be covered.

I am interested in the question of how insurers might be involved in risks of this kind of magnitude, and whether they might be able to help reduce the risk. In the last three years (and particularly in 2026) there have been a number of publications on the question of where insurers might be involved1. In particular, I have drawn heavily from a proposal by the AI Underwriting Company that suggests a mutual insurer set up directly by the labs, but run at arm’s length. I will attempt to summarise these strands of thought and to put some very rough numbers on how much money this would involve, and whether that can indicate if insurers might be able to help address an incentive problem.

I have not tried to address full loss-of-control / human extinction scenarios, but I have tried to check the three scenarios of cyber attacks, pandemic and rogue agent damage. The reason I thought this would be interesting to look at is that if insurers cover these risks, then insurers are incentivised to try to reduce these risks in the same way that life insurance policies might also offer free health checks. While the comparison may make it seem like a long shot (there are huge financial incentives pushing AI development in the “acceleration” direction), I think it’s at least worth exploring how the structures might work and how much money would be involved.

If insurers can change behaviour, four conditions need to be met:

  1. The insurer has enough at stake to care
  2. The lab has reason to accept the insurer’s conditions
  3. The insurer can check whether the lab is complying
  4. The conditions actually improve safety (i.e. aren’t just safety theatre)

To try to answer whether these might hold, it’s necessary to throw some numbers at the question - I have a separate model that you can play around with here.

This has required some fairly heroic / foolish attempts at ball-parking numbers. I’m going to make one, brief apology for this now, at the start, and then leave out the caveats in the rest of the piece. These numbers are definitely wrong, and focussing on them too much tempts spurious accuracy. I believe it’s still a useful exercise - they might be correct in orders of magnitude, and flexing them to see effects on model output can be useful to show which are the most important assumptions. This article is all human-worded, the text on the website is mostly Claude-coded and worded, but I have attempted to put enough detail on the website to explain how the model works if you are interested.

Historical Examples

There are some interesting US historical examples where insurers have arguably been ahead of (both federal and state) government in setting up safety standards and policing them.

  • HSB, now owned by Munich Re had, in 1866, the much grander name of “The Hartford Steam Boiler Inspection and Insurance Company”. Steam boilers had an impressive tendency to explode in the middle of the 1800s. In this case, the product was the other way around - it was primarily an inspection regime with a bonus of an insurance policy on the side.
  • The Price-Anderson Act of 1957 established insurance arrangements to cover public liability from nuclear generator accidents. However, note that this was after government compulsion rather than spontaneously happening pre-government intervention.
  • More recently and perhaps more relevantly to AI risks, cyber risk insurers now require multi factor authentication across all critical systems as a result of experiencing a large growth in ransomware claims in the last decade. However there have been accusations that cyber risk insurers preferred to quickly pay ransoms to ransomware extorters (because it was cheaper than a rebuild), effectively funding the growth of the industry.
  • Another cautionary tale is the National Flood Insurance Program of 1968 which requires towns to adopt floodplain building rules, but the premiums were set lower than actuarial estimates for political reasons, and older properties were exempt from the rules. Thus the lower premiums for older, exempt, properties ended up actually encouraging building on flood plains.

Arguing via analogy, therefore, is it possible that insurers of AI risks could help improve the prospect of AI safety? Can we really imagine a situation where Sam Altman eagerly opens the monthly envelope containing 30% off vouchers for an oversight inspection from Apollo, and thus ChatGPT remains aligned and safe for all? I am actually relatively optimistic about this as a solution, but it’s worth digging into the ways the process might fail.

If you’re choosing who should become the AI Safety police, you broadly have a spectrum of options.

The advantage of a private sector solution is that it is likely to be quicker to set up. The disadvantage is that it is more prone to conflicts of interest. The model of credit ratings agencies being paid to rate companies by those same companies received criticism in the aftermath of the 2007 / 2008 credit / liquidity crisis. Likewise, firm auditors becoming too lenient on their auditees was highlighted post the Worldcom and Enron crises.

The argument in favour of using insurers as part of the solution here is that they are potentially less conflicted. An AI firm buys insurance to cover its risks, and the insurance company is (theoretically) only interested in correctly assessing the risk because it has skin in the game. The insurer, as part of its underwriting process, requires the AI firm to conform to a set of rigorous safety standards that actually reduce the risk of harm. The insurer would therefore themselves pay for the safety audit etc.

This model already, to a certain extent, exists. Anthropic’s S-1 notes that it has liability insurance both for itself as a corporation and on behalf of its directors, but does not go into further detail on its insurance arrangements. The only clue I could see was on page 98, referring to Anthropic’s copyright settlement as part of the Bartz case, where it is implied that their insurance coverage was less than was required to settle the case.

Because of the potential risks, expenses, and uncertainties of litigation or other dispute resolution processes, we may, from time to time, settle disputes, even where we have meritorious claims or defenses, by agreeing to settlement agreements, as we did, for example, in Bartz. Moreover, as in Bartz, insurance may not fully cover such claims, provide sufficient payments to cover all the costs to resolve one or more such claims, or continue to be available on terms acceptable to us.

In even more detail, a June 2026 paper painstakingly identified 26 different insurance products that at least partly referenced AI risks (either explicitly covering AI, or else explicitly excluding AI risk), and broke these risks down into 55 component risks. The authors then filled in the 1,430 squares on the resultant box to indicate what the insurers said publicly about whether the risk was in scope. In this case, the scope is quite wide, covering not primarily AI labs, but the wider set of firms implementing AI as well as building it.

So - perhaps insurance can step in as a de facto regulator while the national and international legal frameworks are still being drafted and debated.

To repeat, insurers might change behaviour, if:

  1. The insurer has enough at stake to care
  2. The lab has reason to accept the insurer’s conditions
  3. The insurer can check whether the lab is complying
  4. The conditions actually improve safety

A Rough Model to Illustrate

To try to estimate to what extent these hold, I think it is helpful to try to put some rough “Fermi estimate” type numbers on this. So I (and, of course, my colleague Claude Code) have put together a fairly simple model of how an actuary might calculate premiums, reserves etc for an AI insurance company.

The model is here. It is deliberately built to be played with, and is not meant to be definitive, however all the assumptions have been documented, and each can be adjusted with the relevant sliders.

I have tried to be as transparent as possible about the model methodology on the website. The model follows a standard actuarial approach: guess how often events occur, and guess how bad they can get. In each case you specify the type of a distribution, and then you pick numbers to get the shape and numbers you want2.

In terms of where to get those parameters from, there are broadly three sources: history, expert/individual judgement and prediction markets. The third is not really independent of the first two, of course. History is fairly limited, and experts differ, often widely. Hence the reason for the sliders, and the heavy caveatting in the previous paragraph.

The types of risk modelled are as follows:

  • An AI-engineered pandemic.
  • A cyber catastrophe enabled by AI.
  • A lab’s own agents directly causing harm in the style of a more serious HuggingFace attack, where OpenAI agents in training broke out of a sandbox environment and hacked an external site.

And another set of key parameters is what the level of maximum cover would be, the structure of the insurance arrangement, whether reinsurers were also involved, and any further risk passed on to the market via catastrophe bonds.

1: The Insurer Has Enough At Stake

To try to put some numbers on the first of our key conditions, whether the insurer has enough at stake to care, let’s look at the modelling of bio risk in detail. Under the central assumptions, there are five labs, with a max of $1bn cover per event each (this is comparable with Swiss Re’s net claims loss from the Christchurch earthquake, for example). AI-enhanced Pandemic risk has been estimated at somewhere between 0.3% and 1.5% per year chance of a pandemic causing more than 100,000 deaths or $1trn in damage. This could be either a deliberate or accidental release. 0.3% was the baseline risk assumed without AI. 1.5% was the risk assuming AI can match top virologists (superforecasters said 0.7%). The central assumption in the model is 0.5% to represent the extra risk above baseline - I’ve picked a number somewhere between the superforecasters’ extra risk (0.4%) and the experts’ (1.2%). The site also has a “Fermi estimator” that the user can use to try to break this probability down into component parts to see if they arrive at a similar order of magnitude.

It’s also necessary to make some assumption at what proportion of damage courts would hold model builders responsible for, and the insurable share. I have chosen fairly low numbers here as default, but in fact these don’t particularly matter for the case of bio risk. In the event of a pandemic, the size of the risk is so large that the maximum payout (in this example $5bn in the case where each lab has $1bn of cover and each is found liable) won’t address the extent of harm. In practice, the insurer would pay out the maximum claim amount, but the remainder of the risk would revert to the lab, and most likely, end up being paid for by society at large.

The insurer is incentivised to care to a certain extent - it will want to reduce the frequency of the risk, but the insurer’s exposure is tiny in comparison to wider society’s.

If we add in the three risks together in terms of how they make up the proportion of the insurer’s headache vs how they determine society’s headache, we get a summary output from the whole model (using our “central” assumptions) as follows.

On a society level - the damage that matters the most is an epidemic. This completely dwarfs a cyber catastrophe (under this set of assumptions). But from the insurer’s point of view, cyber makes up almost two thirds of their claims. If they are acting purely rationally, they will want to focus more of their resource on addressing that, instead of on bio safety.

This is not necessarily fatal for the case, an insurer will still be pro-safety, the point is that the priorities may be different to society’s.

2: The Lab Will Accept the Insurer’s Conditions

Again, under our central assumptions, here is the model output for the cost of the insurance premiums to the labs:

$49m is a tiny proportion of revenue, and that revenue figure is really just a guess of average current revenue across the main five labs. OpenAI and Anthropic have revenues of $50bn or more, currently. And revenues still look to be on a sharply upward trajectory. Even if the insurer offered a 100% discount on cover for complying, if compliance meant a cost of more than $49m (for example delaying a release or running heavier evaluations), it wouldn’t make economic sense for the lab to comply.

On top of that, on the earlier table, the lab’s expectation of insurable liability is $551m, and the cover is expected to pay $77m. So even with insurance, the lab keeps 86% of the risk.

In practice, it won’t be money that will be the incentive for the lab here - it will be compulsion. My instinct is that this second condition only holds if the government forces it to hold through compulsion as in the nuclear industry.

3: The Insurer Can Check Compliance

The model hasn’t been built to look at transparency. However, there is one relevant reflection from building the model. While usually an insurer can look at history to price policies, and keep monitoring or backtesting this with experience, the shape of risk, and its novelty will not really allow this. The underlying parameters came from a mixture of Fermi estimates, expert opinion papers and prediction markets. The insurer is actually therefore even more motivated to check compliance, as it has little else to fall back on to reassure itself that controls are functioning. It’s worth noting that when they investigated the HuggingFace incident, METR had six days on site, with scope set by OpenAI. Currently independent checking only happens on the lab’s terms.

4: Conditions Improve Safety

Rather than focussing on single point estimates for claim totals and so on, we can test the model for the sensitivity of its results to changes in the underlying parameters.

Here is the testing chart for the premium amount, expressed as a proportion of AI revenue (estimated as an average of $25bn for each of the five labs).

The single parameter that makes the largest difference to premium size is the share of cyber risk that is pinned on the lab. This is also a potential source of misaligned incentives, and has relevance to the 4th criterion, whether conditions imposed actually improve safety. The insurer is incentivised to cut the lab’s legal liability as well as improve safety. For instance: tighter terms of contract, contractual caps on what customers can claim, well-structured logs designed to show up well in court, lengthy disclaimers and so on. A rational insurer would push these as part of their conditions even though they don’t reduce overall harm.

However, note that the Forecasting Research Institute, whose estimate of bio risk I used in the model found that safeguards like closed weights and anti-jailbreak measures brought the risk of an engineered pandemic down from 1.25% to 0.4%.

Summary

I think the proposal has legs. But I don’t want to be overly optimistic that this can be a magic bullet. I think the strongest argument is that getting legislation right and getting it enacted is going to take time. The insurance mechanism has the ability to get set up quickly, but would still need some element of legal compulsion. If a mandate from the government requiring insurance cover is a “quick win” legislatively, then insurance can have the best of both worlds as a solution. And while the mechanism is pro-safety in a broad sense, it has the risk of directing incentives on actions that aren’t 100% correlated with reducing harm.


Footnote:

This isn’t meant to be an exhaustive bibliography, but here are some other relevant articles: Cristian Trout argues for following the nuclear model, a proposal for the structure of the insurance stack, the issue with model concentration for insurers, some more suggestions of mechanisms to get pricing and incentives right, the role of catastrophe bonds, an argument for compelling insurance, what to do about restricted access models.

For those who enjoy these things: I have used a Poisson distribution for the frequency of occurrence (with the underlying lambda expectation varying around an inputted value following a gamma distribution), and a Pareto (or power law) distribution for severity. Neither of these choices is particularly controversial, and in particular, the Pareto distribution is a fat-tailed distribution that is fairly standard practice in modelling extreme values / catastrophes. I will gladly take criticism of the model - it’s meant to be an “Aunt Sally” to stress test the four conditions rather than an actual pricing and reserving model for policies. Rather than Aunt Sally - perhaps “Strawman” would make more sense to younger, or non-UK readers. An Aunt Sally is a Victorian fairground game where pub-goers try to knock over a “dolly” with sticks. Please feel free to knock my Aunt Sally down, I won’t mind at all.

item.title: Scott Alexander’s Against SURA Seems Deeply Confused
item.description:
If you are helping build something that might kill everyone, maybe stop doing that.

Ideally, when you do stop, tell everyone else to also stop building it.

That is certainly the obvious, first-level thing to do. You need a damn good reason to decide that no, actually you should keep building the thing that might kill everyone.

Scott Alexander is worried too many people are insisting upon this too loudly. He comes out against a strategy focused on getting people to stop. I disagree. I think many of the claims, arguments and rhetoric in Scott’s post are quite poor by the standards that Scott Alexander would apply to himself.

Scott clearly continues to support advocacy for a global pause, or what he calls Plan A. His objection is to those advocating primarily or exclusively for SURA, which stands for ‘stop unilaterally and raise awareness.’ The practical differences here are smaller than they may at first appear.

This post first lays out my understanding of Scott Alexander’s core claims, then gives my core reactions to those claims, then goes over various questions in detail along with gathering the resulting discussions.

Table of Contents

  1. Scott Alexander’s Core Claims.
  2. My High Level Responses To Scott’s Core Claims.
  3. Briefly on Alignment.
  4. Probabilities and How They Work.
  5. Building a Thing That Might Kill Everyone is Deontologically Evil.
  6. People Quitting Major Labs While Raising Alarms Obviously Works.
  7. On AI Forecasting.
  8. Advancing Capabilities Burns Timeline.
  9. But China.
  10. Ethical People Can Disagree With You.
  11. There Are More Than Two Outcomes.
  12. Efforts Are Complementary, Not Mutually Exclusive.
  13. If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies.
  14. Vaniver is Not Convinced.
  15. There Is No Consensus That We Should Exclusively Focus on Plan A.
  16. It’s Not the Incentives, It’s You.
  17. Anthropic Is Not Optimally Pursuing These Plans.
  18. Against Against Sura.

Scott Alexander’s Core Claims

Scott Alexander writes Against SURA, or the strategy of calling upon nations and companies building superintelligence to stop building it and calling upon employees of those labs to quit, even without reciprocity.

Here is his definition and coinage:

I’ll lump these ideas together under the heading of “SURA” – the idea that the only ethical course is for people/companies/countries to Stop Unilaterally + Raise Awareness, with no plan for what happens if race dynamics continue anyway. I interpret the planks of SURA’s platform as:

  • Individual alignment-pilled AI companies are morally obligated to stop unilaterally, regardless of whether they expect race dynamics to continue in their absence.
  • Individual alignment-pilled employees at these companies should quit, regardless of whether they’re in capabilities or alignment roles, and regardless of whether they think their company is morally better than its competitors.
  • Individual alignment-pilled countries (for example, a hypothetical future alignment-pilled US) should ban or heavily restrict AI progress unilaterally, regardless of whether they expect other countries (for example, China) to continue racing in their absence.

I mostly avoid quoting directly from the OP, since most of you likely read it.

Scott’s basic frame of the situation is that there are two classes of plan:

  1. Plan A, his combination of AI 2040’s Plans A/S/Other, are plans that involve working for a global pause in AI development.
  2. Plan C, his combination of everything else, is where we don’t do that.

Scott’s core arguments are that (this is my ITT summary of Scott):

  1. Many actions that aim to help your chances of pulling off Plan A hurt your chances of survival if Plan A fails and you are forced back into Plan C.
    1. Plan C benefits from ‘alignment-pilling’ the companies, whereas Plan A benefits from raising mass awareness, educating politicians and getting verification tech.
    2. SURA is one of the actions that hurts Plan C.
  2. Plan A is first best, and we should try to do it, but it probably won’t happen, and a large portion of our victories come from executing Plan C.
  3. The correct and traditional strategy is to support Plan A while also preparing to execute Plan C as best we can.
  4. SURA, telling whoever listens to unilaterally stop, de facto torches our chances for execution of Plan C in order to maximize the chances of getting to try Plan A.
  5. SURA is an increasingly popular strategy, but it only makes sense if you believe some combination of assumptions.
    1. Alignment is highly doomed, or is highly doomed under Plan C conditions.
    2. Racing to superintelligence under these conditions is deontologically evil.
    3. Racing burns valuable time.
    4. People quitting is helpful in raising awareness and pursuing a pause.
  6. SURA is actually bad for even your chances of getting Plan A.
  7. There is currently a ‘consensus in favor of SURA’ in rationalist/EA spaces.

Scott also makes other claims, such as his overview of alignment. In many cases the claims seem overgeneralized or overstated.

I respond to Scott’s claims, and without any implicit endorsement of claims I do not mention.

My High Level Responses To Scott’s Core Claims

  1. True in general, but often false for specific actions where it is claimed.
    1. These actions all help both Plan A and Plan C, although they differentially help their respective plans more.
    2. If fully executed, yes. On the margin, the sign of impact is not obvious.
  2. True, given our uncertainty over the situation. I agree with Scott Alexander that this is his strongest point.
    1. There are those who disagree, and I respect the opposite position.
  3. True for the world overall, in aggregate. Not obviously true for an individual or group, and not obviously true on the margin.
  4. Extreme forms of SURA can be negative for Plan C, but on net and on the margin while sign is unclear I expect reasonable ones to be positive even for Plan C.
  5. These are key arguments in favor of SURA, but even if all four were false it would not definitively render SURA a bad idea, as this is not an exhaustive list.
    1. I have high model uncertainty on this. I respect those who think alignment under Plan C is highly doomed. They have good arguments. I am not fully convinced. Alignment under Plan C could turn out to be highly doomed, or building superintelligence could be highly doomed even if alignment is solved, or it is possible that alignment is ‘super doable’ although difficult.
    2. I am not a deontologist, but yeah, it seems rather deontologically evil. You might want to do it anyway, and at some point in a cost-benefit analysis you have to be willing to as Rao says Be Slightly Evil, but don’t pretend otherwise.

Against Against Sura

For the purposes of discussing what to do next, let us break up SURA into Absurd SURA, Strong SURA and Weak SURA, and then there is non-SURA.

Absurd SURA says the only ethical or valid action is to tell countries to ban AI capabilities development, labs to shut down and employees to quit.

I call it ‘Absurd SURA’ because this is an obviously dumb strawman. Disregard.

Strong SURA says the only ethical or valid action is to stop developing AI capabilities. Ideally one would coordinate with other nations or labs to do so. But, failing that, nations must ban AI capabilities development, labs must shut down and employees must quit. It is not worth investing in a fallback plan, and indeed it is at least arguably better not to help the labs with their prosaic alignment as this prevents warning shots.

I think this is a valid position to take. It is right if one believes that prosaic alignment plans as could potentially be implemented by Anthropic or OpenAI are doomed. As in, if you think that a realistic ‘Plan C+’ very likely causes everyone to die.

Weak SURA says that you should fight hard for Plan A and for a coordinated pause, that on the margin more employees should loudly quit, and that if coordination is unsuccessful then labs and nations should soon point pause even on their own, if capabilities advance the way the labs predict they will advance. But that a better execution of Plan C can matter a lot too, so you should also simultaneously strive to maximize our chances of a good execution of Plan C.

Non-SURA is opposed even to Weak SURA, and prefers to optimize Plan C. It tries to back ‘the good guys’ which typically means America and Anthropic, and to ensure they have as big a lead as possible.

Scott Alexander spends his post arguing against at least Strong SURA.

My position on this is that I respect advocates of Strong SURA, I am walking the path of Weak SURA, and I reject both Absurd SURA and non-SURA.

Should you treat lab employees as deontologically evil people? I say no. Nor do you need to shun or be rude to them. But I do think you should treat them, whether or not they have good reason to do it, as participating in a deontologically evil thing. When you are building a thing that might kill everyone there might be no better play available, but also you should seriously consider maybe not doing that.
